AI native, never AI only: AI in a component library that never calls a model
Why Peacock's AI components never talk to a model, how one switch removes AI cleanly, and how drafts, labels and allow-lists keep people in control.

import Figure from "../../components/mdx/Figure.astro"; import Callout from "../../components/mdx/Callout.astro"; import AiBoundary from "../../components/diagrams/AiBoundary.astro"; Redvars, the platform I'm building, has one rule about AI: **AI native, never AI only.** The assistant acts as the person using it. It can read freely, it only ever writes drafts that the person confirms, and every page has to work completely with AI switched off. Apps on Redvars build their pages with [Peacock](/blog/peacock-architecture/), which puts a lot of that rule in Peacock's hands. Peacock decides how suggested values, drafts, generated text, citations and streaming answers look and behave, and whether switching AI off really makes them go away. This is how I designed it: a component library that supports an assistant everywhere, but never calls a model itself. ## Where I started Before this work, Peacock had no AI pieces at all. Every app would have drawn its own "suggested" marker, found its own way to stream text, and reached a model on its own. The platform rule would have been honoured differently on every page, or not at all. ## The options Leaving it to apps meant nothing to build. But every app would draw its own markers and call its own model, and the platform rule forbids exactly that. Components that call a model themselves, with an `endpoint` property and a built-in client, make for quick demos. They also open a second road to a model, next to the platform's model service, with its own credentials and no access checks. The third option was model-free components with one registered provider. Components show whatever AI state the app passes in, and the few interactive features call a single provider that the app registers. The third. Peacock never calls a model. It renders AI state and asks one provider for text, so credentials, access checks and the choice of model all stay in the platform, where they belong. ## How it works ### Most of it is just properties Most AI features only need to show something: a field's `suggestion`, a summary's `value` while it's `streaming`, a list of `citations`, a draft card's `state`. The app sets these like any other property. That works with any backend and doesn't need a provider at all. ### A few features ask for text A handful of features do need to ask for text: ghost text while you type, rewriting a selection, summarising, and turning a sentence into filters. They call the provider registered for the page: ```js import { setPeacockAi } from "https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/@redvars/peacock@4.5.1/dist/loader.js"; setPeacockAi({ provider: { complete: ({ before, after, signal }) => myModel.complete(before, after, { signal }), transform: ({ action, text, instruction, signal }) => myModel.stream(action, text, instruction, { signal }), summarize: ({ kind, text, signal }) => myModel.stream("summarize", text, kind, { signal }), parse: ({ target, text, schema, signal }) => myModel.json(target, text, schema, { signal }), }, }); ``` Every method is optional, and a feature only appears when its method exists. Each call gets an `AbortSignal` and a context that holds only the text that component owns. Streams are `AsyncIterable`. ### Switching AI off `setPeacockAi({ enabled: false })` turns AI off for the whole page. To drop a single capability, call it again without that capability, for example `setPeacockAi({ provider, features: { summarize: false } })`. Each call replaces the whole configuration, so the provider has to come along. Any element with `no-ai` opts out on its own. When AI is off, anything that refers to the assistant renders nothing: badges, "Ask" buttons, AI menu groups. Interactive features aren't offered. The neutral pieces keep working, because they were never really about AI. A typing indicator also shows people typing, a citation is just a reference to a record, and streaming Markdown is just streaming. ### AI output is always labelled There's one marker, `wc-ai-badge`, with three states: `suggested` for a value the person hasn't accepted yet, `draft` for something waiting for confirmation, and `generated` for read-only output such as a summary. It always carries text, never colour alone. It can show a `reason`, and it can be cleared in one action. ### The assistant only writes drafts No component turns AI output into a committed value without the person doing something. Ghost text needs Tab, a rewrite needs Accept, and a draft card needs Confirm. If the draft can't be undone, it asks a second time. Suggested values work the same way. Give a form control `suggestion = { value, reason }` and it holds the value, shows a Suggested badge with the reason, and remembers what it replaced. Editing the value, or submitting the form, accepts it. The badge's clear button puts the old value back. ### Where the trust lines are A field marked `sensitive` is never sent to the provider, and its AI features are hidden. Password and PIN fields are always sensitive. Model text is treated as untrusted. It only reaches the screen through `wc-markdown`, which renders raw HTML as text and allows only safe links, or through `wc-generative-view`. Nothing executes it or submits it on its own. Citations never follow URLs a model wrote. A citation is written `[1](cite:record-id)`, and the app looks up the record itself. ### Generative view: what it refuses matters most `wc-generative-view` shows an answer as Peacock components described by JSON nodes, for answers that read better as a chart or a table than as text. The data comes from the platform; the model only arranges it. What keeps it safe is everything it refuses to render. It renders only a hand-kept catalog of components and props. A test fails if the committed catalog is stale, or if it allows a prop that can navigate, load an address or run code, such as `href`, `src` or a callback. Anything outside the catalog is dropped and reported. A view stops at 12 levels and 500 nodes, and text is never parsed as HTML. And `generativeViewSchema()` hands the catalog to the model service as a JSON Schema for structured output, so the model is only asked for what the view can actually render. ### Accessibility Streaming text sets `aria-busy` and is announced once, when it's complete, not word by word. Indicators use `role="status"`, and the motion stops under `prefers-reduced-motion`. ## What it cost Some things got easier. Every app labels AI output the same way. Switching AI off is one call. Changing model providers happens in the platform and nowhere else. And components can be tested with a scripted provider, no model required. Some things got harder. Every AI-enhanced component has to be designed and tested twice, once with AI on and once with it off. The provider contract is public API now, too, so it follows the same deprecation rules as everything else. Text inside records can steer a model, and Peacock can't stop that. What it can do is limit the damage: model output becomes drafts that a person has to confirm, and text is rendered without HTML. The assistant's own defences belong to the platform. ## The short version Putting AI into a component library turned out to be mostly about where you draw the lines. Peacock's are easy to say out loud. The library never calls a model. Anything AI wrote is labelled. Every write is a draft. And every page still works when AI is switched off.
Bus reservation system: database design and ER diagram
My bus reservation system, written up properly: the requirements, the ER diagram, the MySQL schema, the one unique index that stops double booking, and how the Java Swing app sits on Spring JDBC.

import Figure from "../../components/mdx/Figure.astro"; import Callout from "../../components/mdx/Callout.astro"; import BusReservationER from "../../components/diagrams/BusReservationER.astro"; In 2014 I built a bus reservation system as my academic mini project: a desktop app where passengers find buses on a route, pick their seats and cancel tickets. It's written in Java, with a Swing interface, Spring JDBC and MySQL, and the [code is on GitHub](https://github.com/shivajivarma/bus-reservation-system). The old page about it is one of the most visited on this site, so I've rewritten it properly: the requirements, the ER diagram, the schema and the constraints that keep the data honest, how the app is put together, and what I'd do differently now. ## What it had to fix Picture a bus operator that books on paper. Someone has to keep several records in step by hand: which buses run on which route, what each one costs and when it leaves, and which seats are taken on which date. Finding anything means flipping through the books. Mistakes in seat allocation or billing turn into arguments with customers, and paper is hard to keep secure. The goal was one shared database that every booking goes through, so that: - a passenger can check availability and pick specific seats, - no seat is ever sold twice, - a ticket can be cancelled by the person who booked it, and - every booking leaves a record that a ticket can be printed from. ## What the app does My original project write-up named three modules: enquiry, reservation and cancellation. Accounts and a ticket history round it out. | Module | What it does | Database work | | --- | --- | --- | | Accounts | Register and sign in | Insert into `passenger`; look up by username | | Enquiry | Find buses and free seats for a route and date | Read `route`, `bus` and `reserve` | | Reservation | Book one or more seats and print the tickets | Insert one `reserve` row per seat | | Cancellation | Cancel a ticket by its number | Delete the `reserve` row, if it's yours | | History | List past tickets and reprint them | Read the `reservation` view | ## Finding the entities Read the requirements looking for nouns and four entities fall out: - **Route**: an origin and a destination. - **Bus**: a service on one route, with a fare, AC or not, and departure and arrival times. - **Passenger**: an account with a username, password, name, email and mobile number. - **Reservation**: one seat, on one bus, on one date, booked by one passenger. In the schema it's the `reserve` table, and every row is a ticket. Two things sound like entities but aren't tables. A seat is just a number from 1 to 40, because every bus has the same 40-seat layout. And a trip is just a bus plus a date. The model assumes each bus runs its route every day, so a reservation only needs the bus and the travel date to pin down the journey. That saves a trip table and a join in every query. The price is flexibility: buses that skip days, or fares that change by date, would need a real `trip` table. ## The ER diagram Here's how to read it: - A route is served by zero or more buses, and each bus runs exactly one route: `bus.routeid` is a required foreign key to `route.id`. - A passenger makes zero or more reservations, and each reservation belongs to exactly one passenger. - A bus carries zero or more reservations, and each one is for exactly one bus. Step back and passengers and buses are many-to-many: a passenger rides many buses, and a bus carries many passengers. `reserve` breaks that into two one-to-many relationships, and it's also where the facts about each pairing live: the travel date (`dt`), the seat, and the date it was booked (`tstamp`). ## The schema These are the table definitions from `db/setup.sql`, tidied up a little. The script creates them in a schema called `brs`, which is the database the app connects to. ```sql CREATE TABLE route ( id INT NOT NULL AUTO_INCREMENT, origin VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL, destination VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL, PRIMARY KEY (id) ) AUTO_INCREMENT = 10; CREATE UNIQUE INDEX ROUTE_UNIQUE ON route (origin, destination); CREATE TABLE bus ( id INT NOT NULL AUTO_INCREMENT, routeid INT NOT NULL, ac BOOLEAN NOT NULL, fare INT NOT NULL, departuretime VARCHAR(6) NOT NULL, arrivaltime VARCHAR(6) NOT NULL, PRIMARY KEY (id), FOREIGN KEY (routeid) REFERENCES route (id) ) AUTO_INCREMENT = 200; CREATE TABLE passenger ( id INT NOT NULL AUTO_INCREMENT, username VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL UNIQUE, password VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL, name VARCHAR(40) NOT NULL, email VARCHAR(32) NOT NULL, mobile BIGINT NOT NULL, PRIMARY KEY (id) ) AUTO_INCREMENT = 500; CREATE TABLE reserve ( id INT NOT NULL AUTO_INCREMENT, passengerid INT NOT NULL, busid INT NOT NULL, dt DATE NOT NULL, -- travel date tstamp DATE NOT NULL, -- date of booking seat INT NOT NULL, PRIMARY KEY (id), FOREIGN KEY (passengerid) REFERENCES passenger (id), FOREIGN KEY (busid) REFERENCES bus (id) ) AUTO_INCREMENT = 1000; CREATE UNIQUE INDEX SEAT_UNIQUE ON reserve (busid, dt, seat); ``` Two details are easy to miss. Each table starts counting from its own number: routes from 10, buses from 200, passengers from 500 and tickets from 1000. While the tables are small, an id tells you on its own which table it came from, and every ticket number has at least four digits. And departure and arrival times are plain text, like `'20:00'`. The app only ever displays them. ## Constraints that do the real work Three unique indexes carry the business rules: | Constraint | Rule it enforces | | --- | --- | | `ROUTE_UNIQUE (origin, destination)` | Each route is listed once | | `passenger.username UNIQUE` | No two accounts share a username | | `SEAT_UNIQUE (busid, dt, seat)` | A seat on a bus is sold once per date | The seat screen loads the seats that are already taken and disables them. That alone isn't enough: two people can open the same bus at the same moment and both see seat 12 as free. The unique index on `(busid, dt, seat)` means the database turns down the second booking, whatever either screen showed. I added it in the 2.0 rewrite. Registration works the same way on a smaller scale. The app checks that a username is free before inserting, and the `UNIQUE` constraint backs that check up. ## Counting free seats The bus list shows how many seats are left on each bus for the date you picked. There's no counter column to keep in step; the query just counts reservations as it reads. Here it is, simplified from `BusDAOImpl`: ```sql SELECT id, ac, departuretime, arrivaltime, fare, (SELECT 40 - COUNT(*) FROM reserve WHERE busid = bus.id AND dt = ?) AS availability FROM bus WHERE routeid IN (SELECT id FROM route WHERE origin = ? AND destination = ?); ``` Because availability is worked out rather than stored, it can never disagree with the reservations. It costs one count per bus per search, and since `SEAT_UNIQUE` already starts with `(busid, dt)`, that count is an index lookup. ## The reservation view The History tab shows each ticket with its route and times, and those live in two other tables. A view joins them once. Here it is with explicit joins; its `ORDER BY` is what keeps the History tab in order: ```sql CREATE VIEW reservation AS SELECT reserve.id, reserve.passengerid, reserve.busid, reserve.seat, reserve.dt, reserve.tstamp, route.origin, route.destination, bus.departuretime, bus.arrivaltime FROM reserve JOIN bus ON reserve.busid = bus.id JOIN route ON bus.routeid = route.id ORDER BY reserve.id; ``` The app reads a passenger's history with one query against the view and maps each row straight onto a `ReservationBean`, the same object the printed ticket is built from. ## Booking a ticket, step by step | Step | Screen | What happens in the database | | --- | --- | --- | | 1 | Sign in | Look up `passenger` by username; the app compares the password | | 2 | Reservation tab | List origins that have at least one bus, then their destinations; the app requires a future date | | 3 | Bus selection | Run the availability query above | | 4 | Seat selection | Load the seats taken for that bus and date, and disable them in a grid of 40 seats, four to a row | | 5 | Book | Insert one `reserve` row per selected seat, then print the tickets as an HTML page | | 6 | Cancel tab | Load the ticket, and delete it only if it belongs to the signed-in passenger | Origins come from `SELECT DISTINCT origin FROM route WHERE id IN (SELECT routeid FROM bus)`, so a route with no buses never shows up in the drop-downs. ## How the code is organised There are four layers, a package each: - **Views** (`ui`): Swing panels, one per screen. - **Controllers** (`controller`): one per screen, connecting view events to services. `MasterController` swaps panels in the main window as you move between screens. `HomeTabsMediator` creates the Reservation, Cancel and History tabs and keeps them in step; for example, it refreshes the history when you switch tabs. - **Services** (`model.service`): rules like "only the passenger who booked a ticket can cancel it". - **Data access** (`model.dao`): the SQL, built on Spring's `JdbcDaoSupport` and `JdbcTemplate`. `BeanPropertyRowMapper` maps rows onto entity classes, and `spring-jdbc.xml` wires the data source into each DAO. The first public release, in May 2015, ran against Oracle. Spring JDBC came that June. The 2.0 rewrite in autumn 2015 reorganised the code into these layers, moved the build to Maven and the database to MySQL, and added the seat index. In 2023 I updated the dependencies and added a GitHub Actions build. ## What I'd change today Looking at the code again now, here's what I'd change. **Under load.** I'd read each new ticket number from the insert's generated key. Right now the app runs `SELECT MAX(id)` straight after inserting, which can hand back someone else's ticket if two bookings land at the same moment. I'd also book all the selected seats in one transaction and turn the duplicate-key error into a friendly "that seat was just taken". As it stands, each seat is inserted on its own, so a failure halfway through leaves the earlier seats booked and prints no tickets. **Security.** Passwords are stored as plain text and compared in the app. They should be hashed with something deliberately slow, like bcrypt or Argon2. **The data model.** I'd record the fare on each reservation; it lives only on the bus, so the price someone actually paid isn't kept. I'd use proper types: `TIME` for departure and arrival, `DATETIME` for when a ticket was booked (`tstamp` is a `DATE`, so the time of day is lost), and real dates instead of strings parsed with `STR_TO_DATE`. Each bus would get a capacity, instead of the number 40 written into both the availability query and the seat screen. And cancelled tickets would get a status column instead of being deleted, so there's an audit trail and something to report on. **The application.** One Spring context for the whole app, and a connection pool. Today each service builds its own context, and `DriverManagerDataSource` opens a fresh connection for every query. The schema has held up better than the code around it. What still stands is what the database enforces: required foreign keys, unique indexes, and availability counted from the reservations instead of stored beside them. Most of my list is that same lesson taken further. Let the database hand out keys and guard transactions, and keep the facts the business will want later, like what a ticket cost. ## Run it yourself The source is on [GitHub](https://github.com/shivajivarma/bus-reservation-system). You'll need Java 8 or later, Maven and MySQL. One warning first: the app was built on Windows and assumes it in two places. Printed tickets are saved to `%APPDATA%` and opened with a Windows command. And the SQL in the app writes table names in mixed case, like `Bus`, which MySQL on Windows doesn't mind. On Linux, MySQL treats table names as case sensitive by default, so those queries fail. 1. Clone the repository: `git clone https://github.com/shivajivarma/bus-reservation-system.git` 2. Create a MySQL user `admin` with the password `admin`, or put your own credentials in `src/main/resources/spring-jdbc.xml`. 3. Run `db/setup.sql`, then `db/data.sql`. The data adds 12 routes between Visakhapatnam, Hyderabad, Bangalore and Tirupati, and 11 buses. 4. Import the project into your IDE as a Maven project, build it, and run `com.shivajivarma.brs.AppLauncher`. 5. Register an account on the first screen, then book a seat.
Writing the rules before writing 46 more components
How an audit of Peacock's 85 components turned into one decision record: when to split a component, one event contract, one vocabulary, and what the migration cost.

import Figure from "../../components/mdx/Figure.astro"; import Callout from "../../components/mdx/Callout.astro"; import EventFunnel from "../../components/diagrams/EventFunnel.astro"; ## Eight ways to say "close" By late 2026, [Peacock](/blog/peacock-architecture/) had about 85 components, written over several years. The roadmap in front of me added roughly 46 more and reworked most of the existing ones. Every pattern already in the library was about to be copied dozens of times, so it felt like the right moment to stop and look at what I had. I audited the old components before writing any new ones, and the same ideas kept turning up spelled different ways. "Close" had eight event names: `closed`, `modal-close`, `side-sheet-close`, `snackbar-close`, `notification-dismiss`, `tag--dismiss` and two more. Fields fired three different event shapes, so code that read one field's value broke on the next. `variant` meant visual style on buttons and meaning on alerts. And some modes dragged along options that did nothing: `wc-input type="password"` and `wc-date-field range` both carried settings that were dead in the component's other modes. None of these is a bug. Put together, though, they make a library you have to look up instead of learn. ## Three ways forward I could fix things case by case. That costs nothing today, but every phase of the roadmap would argue about the same questions again, and the drift would carry on. I could adopt another design system's API wholesale, say Material Web or Shoelace. It would be consistent, sure, but their names clash with Peacock's, and switching would break more than it fixed. Or I could write Peacock's own conventions, based on what most components already did, and bring the rest in line through deprecations. The third. If the rules describe what the majority already does, most components are compliant on day one. The rest would migrate through a deprecation window in 3.x, and the old names would go in one major release, 4.0. ## The rules ### When a mode becomes its own component A mode becomes a separate component when it changes the value you read or write, or when it brings options that do nothing in the other modes. It stays an option only when it mirrors a native HTML attribute (`multiple`, `disabled`, `required`) and every other option still applies. Questions that used to be judgement calls now have an answer. `wc-password-field` and `wc-date-range-field` became components. `wc-select multiple` stayed an option. ### One event contract Value controls fire `input` while the value changes and `change` when it's committed. Both are `CustomEvent<{ value }>`, and controls that hold several values add `values`. Overlays and disclosures fire `open` and `close`, and `close` says why in `detail.reason`. Event names are plain kebab-case verbs, never `component-name-verb` or `block--modifier`, and every custom event bubbles and crosses shadow boundaries. ### One vocabulary Same idea, same word, everywhere: | Concept | Name | | --- | --- | | Visual style | `variant` | | Meaning | `intent`: `info`, `success`, `warning`, `danger` | | Chosen item | `selected` | | Current location | `current` | | Accessible name | `label` | | Overlay position | `placement`, logical: `top`, `bottom`, `start`, `end` | | Can be closed by the user | `dismissible` | | Open state | `open`, with `show()`, `hide()`, `toggle()` | | Busy | `loading` | | Size | one scale, `sm`, `md`, `lg`, the same height on buttons and fields | One small rule does more than you'd expect: booleans default to `false`. That way you can switch any boolean on from HTML just by adding the attribute. If a feature is on by default, its attribute is spelled as the opposite, like `hide-toolbar`. Rules like this are easiest to apply to new components. A few older ones, such as the code editor's line numbers, still need converting. ### Deprecate first, break once Renamed and removed APIs kept working through the whole 3.x line. An old name logs one console warning per page, and its docs page lists it. 4.0 removed them all and shipped with a migration guide. ## How it shipped There was no big migration project. Each phase of the roadmap brought the components it touched into line, so the cleanup rode along with work that was happening anyway. Peacock 4.0 then removed the shims and shipped one event contract, one vocabulary, one size scale and logical placements across the library, plus more than 50 new components built to the same rules. ## What changed Some things got easier. Learn one component and you can guess the next. Code reviews check against a list instead of someone's taste. Even the generated [React, Vue and Angular packages](/blog/generate-dont-handwrite/) got simpler, because there's only one event shape to map to two-way binding. Some got harder. Existing components needed renames and deprecation shims, people saw console warnings until they migrated, and a major version had to carry the cleanup. An API convention is architecture, even though it never runs. Write it before a big build-out and it shapes every new component at no extra cost. Write it afterwards and you're migrating everything you just built.
Generate, don't hand-write: one manifest, three framework packages
Field notes on generating Peacock's React, Vue and Angular packages from custom-elements.json: the rules it puts on component authors, and the tests that keep generated code honest.

import Callout from "../../components/mdx/Callout.astro";

## Why wrappers at all

[Peacock](/blog/peacock-architecture/)'s components are custom elements, so they already render
inside React, Vue and Angular. What people miss in those frameworks is the native feel: typed
props, typed events, and two-way binding that works with each framework's own forms.

```tsx
import "@redvars/peacock/styles.css";
import { Input } from "@redvars/peacock-react";

<Input label="Name" value={name} onInput={(event) => setName(event.detail.value)} />;
```

Writing that layer by hand for three frameworks and nearly two hundred elements means keeping three
copies of every API in step. They'd drift apart the first time someone forgot one. So nobody
writes it.

## The manifest is the contract

The build analyses the components into `custom-elements.json`. A generator script reads that
manifest and writes each framework package's bindings into its `src/generated` folder. The rest of
each package is small and kept by hand: its `package.json`, the entry file that re-exports the
bindings, and a demo app. Every generated file starts with a header that says where it came from
and asks you not to edit it.

The consequence I care about most is this: **a component's public API is whatever the analyzer can
see.** If it isn't in the manifest, it isn't public.

## What it asks of component authors

These rules live in the component guidelines, because the generator depends on them.

Public, writable fields become props, so internals get a `_` prefix or are marked `private` or
`readonly` to keep them out of the bindings.

Every event is documented with `@fires name` and a `CustomEvent<Detail>` type, and the detail type
is exported. Skip that and the bindings fall back to `CustomEvent<unknown>`.

Two-way binding is detected, not declared. A component gets it when it has `value` plus an `input`
or `change` event whose detail has `value`, or `checked` plus `change`.

Tag names are written out literally in templates (`<wc-icon`), never built from strings, because
the bindings work out which elements a component renders by scanning its source.

```ts
/**
 * @fires {CustomEvent<{ value: string }>} input - Dispatched while the value changes.
 * @fires {CustomEvent<{ value: string }>} change - Dispatched when the value is committed.
 */
```

<Callout kind="lesson">
  The [API conventions](/blog/component-api-conventions/) and the generator prop each other up. One
  event contract means one rule for two-way binding, and a generator that depends on that contract
  makes the convention hard to break.
</Callout>

## What comes out

Each package gets a **registration layer**: one module per tag that defines the element plus the
tags it renders. Import `Input` and `wc-input` is registered along with everything inside it, so a
framework app never loads `loader.js`.

On top of that, each framework gets its own idiom:

| Package | Two-way binding |
| --- | --- |
| `@redvars/peacock-react` | `value` and `checked` with `onInput` and `onChange` |
| `@redvars/peacock-vue` | `v-model` |
| `@redvars/peacock-angular` | `ngModel`, `formControl`, `formControlName` |

## Keeping generated code honest

Generated code tends to fail quietly. A missing event type doesn't break the build; it just makes
the types weaker. Two kinds of tests watch for that. Generator tests (`node --test`) run after any
change to a component's API. And a smoke test builds a small demo app for each framework, serves
it, and drives it in Chrome with Puppeteer, so the bindings get checked in a real browser, the way
an app would use them.

## Once you trust it, you see it everywhere

Generation shows up in other corners of Peacock too. The theme engine is plain ESM with no
Node-only imports, so the same code builds `tokens.css` in Node and runs the docs theme builder in
the browser, and the two can't disagree. The generative view's catalog, the allow-list of
components that AI answers may render, takes each prop's type, enum values and description from
the component manifest. A test fails when the committed catalog goes stale.

## Notes to self

- Generate from something the build already produces and checks, so there's no second source to
  keep in sync.
- Put the generator's assumptions in the authoring guidelines, where component authors will
  actually read them.
- Test generated code in the runtime it targets, not just with the compiler.
One door to the data: how Redvars enforces security
Every read and write in Redvars goes through one path, a persistence layer that asks one authorizer before it touches storage. Why that matters, and what gets enforced along the way.

import Figure from "../../components/mdx/Figure.astro"; import Callout from "../../components/mdx/Callout.astro"; import DataPath from "../../components/diagrams/DataPath.astro"; Security that's applied at the edge gets bypassed eventually, usually by an internal caller nobody was thinking about: a background job, a script, an admin tool. In [Redvars](/blog/redvars-platform-architecture/) there's exactly one door to the data, and everything goes through it: the gateway, the UI, a rule's action, a custom page, the AI assistant. ## The path Entry points get in only through the kernel's public API, which authenticates the caller into a session bound to one identity and one scope. From there, every read and write goes through persistence, and persistence's security handler asks the authorizer before it touches storage. Because there's one choke point, role checks, auditing, validation and rule triggering can't be skipped, and each of them is implemented exactly once. The structure enforces it, too. Modules can change what the kernel does, but daemons can only call it, so an entry point can never get a privileged path to data. It's simply never handed one. ## Real tables, not EAV Persistence is part of the kernel, so it's always loaded. It lets people create tables, fields and relationships at runtime, and it runs every record read and write. Each table someone defines becomes a real PostgreSQL table, namespaced per application and described by a metadata catalog. Not entity-attribute-value rows, and not one JSON blob per record. Real tables get indexes, constraints, joins, the query planner and ordinary tooling for reporting and backups. EAV is slow and hostile to SQL, and a single JSONB column gives up integrity. Adding or changing a field produces an ordered, transactional DDL migration, recorded in the catalog. Destructive changes, like dropping a column or narrowing a type, are explicit and gated. Every table gets the same system columns: an id, who created and last updated it and when, a version number, a soft-delete flag, and a domain column on tables that use [domain separation](/blog/one-instance-per-organisation/). The version is for optimistic concurrency. Enterprise forms stay open for a long time, so locking would hurt; instead a lost update is detected when it's saved. And enterprise data is rarely truly deleted, so soft delete plus an audit trail is worth the storage. Queries are structured descriptions (a filter, a sort, the fields to return, related records to expand, a page) compiled to parameterised SQL. SQL is never built as a string from user input. ## Who you are, and what you may do Identity and access are two modules. `identity` works out who the caller is: users, groups, credentials, sign-in. Authenticators stack, tried in order (passwords, then SSO, then API keys), and each one produces the same kind of identity. `access` decides what that identity may do, and there's only ever one of it. The model is RBAC. Users belong to groups, groups hold roles, roles grant permissions, and a permission is a resource plus an operation, optionally with conditions. Resources range from tables and fields down to single records, pages, workflows and admin functions. The default is deny: no permission, no access. Roles only ever add, so nobody has to puzzle out whether a deny beats an allow. Record-level conditions, such as `owner = $user` or `department in $user.departments`, become part of the query's WHERE clause, so the database does the filtering. Filtering after fetching leaks counts, breaks pagination and doesn't scale. Pushing it into the query makes the secure path the fast path as well. ## Closing the gaps A few smaller decisions close the holes that usually appear around a model like this. The two built-in roles live in code, not in rows. `admin` is for an organisation's administrators. `root` is for platform development; an organisation's own users never hold it, and it can't be granted anywhere but a developer's own machine. Rows are data, and an administrator could delete them and lock every other administrator out. Code is fixed, visible and tested. A module can mark one of its tables as restricted in its schema: password hashes, session secrets, who owns what. Then no ACL and no administrator can reach it. A list kept as data could be edited by the very people it restricts, but a schema only changes with its module's release. PostgreSQL row-level security sits behind the authorizer, so a bug in a module isn't enough to leak another domain's rows. Decisions are cached per identity and dropped when roles change. Every denial and every privileged action is logged. And when an administrator acts as someone else, the session keeps the real person alongside, every audit column is filled in as the person being acted as, and every page shows a banner for as long as it lasts. ## The assistant is just another caller This is also why the AI assistant fitted in safely. It calls the kernel's API in the person's own session, like any other caller, so the authorizer decides every read and write. It has no identity or access of its own, so it can never do more than the person using it could. There's more on that in [AI native, never AI only](/blog/ai-native-components/). ## What it costs One path means one place to get right, so that place has to be fast: real indexed tables, authorization pushed into SQL, and cached metadata and decisions. Runtime schema changes are operationally sensitive, because a migration can lock a large table, so they use online-safe patterns and limits during peak load. Very large tables are a problem for after the first release. And pure RBAC can sprawl into too many roles. Groups and condition templates keep that in check. If an organisation ever needs richer policy, based on time, location or relationships, a different module that provides the authorizer can replace `access` without any caller changing. ## The one rule I'd keep If I could keep only one rule from all of Redvars, it would be this one. There's one door to the data, and everyone has to come through it, including the platform's own parts.
One instance per organisation: tenancy in Redvars
Why every organisation that uses Redvars gets its own database and deployment instead of a shared multi-tenant platform, and how a service provider can still run many organisations from one instance.

import Figure from "../../components/mdx/Figure.astro"; import Callout from "../../components/mdx/Callout.astro"; import DomainTree from "../../components/diagrams/DomainTree.astro"; Every platform that serves more than one organisation has to answer the same question early: do they share the system, or does each one get its own? It's one of those decisions that's cheap to make and very expensive to change, because the answer ends up in every query, cache key and queued job. For [Redvars](/blog/redvars-platform-architecture/), I chose one instance per organisation. This is why, and how service providers who look after many organisations still fit. ## Two ways to serve many organisations Shared multi-tenancy puts everyone in one deployment and tells them apart with a tenant key. It's cheap to run, but that key has to be threaded through every query, every cache entry and every job, forever. Forget it once and one organisation sees another's data. An instance per organisation gives each one its own deployment: its own PostgreSQL database, its own cache, its own runtime nodes. Isolation comes from the infrastructure, not from code remembering to filter. An instance per organisation. The platform has no concept of a tenant at all, and no database ever holds more than one organisation's data. ## Why It's the strongest isolation for the least engineering. Data, noisy neighbours and the blast radius of a bad day are all separated by default, and there's no tenant key to thread through anything. Each organisation also gets its own upgrade schedule, its own data residency, and its own backup and restore. And it's what enterprises tend to ask for anyway. On a host, instances live side by side in a project folder. Each one has a folder of its own for its configuration, secrets, logs and application cache, and they share only the platform releases, which never change once they're unpacked. So sharing a release can't let one instance break another. It isn't free. A fleet of instances needs tooling to provision, upgrade and monitor them that a shared platform wouldn't. I treat that as an operations problem that sits outside the core runtime, and how that tooling works across many hosts is still an open question. ## Keeping instances apart in the browser, too There's a less obvious kind of isolation. Instances run pages and scripts their owners write, so the browser is part of the security boundary too. Redvars leans on what modern browsers already enforce, and uses it strictly. The login session lives in one cookie. It's `HttpOnly`, so page scripts never see it. It carries the `__Secure-` prefix, so browsers only accept it over HTTPS. It's `SameSite=Strict` and limited to the API's path, so it isn't sent with requests that start on another site. And it's set without a `Domain`, so it belongs to the instance's own host and nothing else. Any request that rides on that cookie and changes something has to come from the instance's own origin, or one an administrator has listed, and has to carry an `X-Requested-With` header, which a cross-site form can't send. Sign-in calls get the same check, so a hostile page can't even log a browser in. Other origins get no credentialed CORS access unless they're explicitly allowed; by default it's same origin only. Application pages go one step further. They run in a sandboxed iframe without same-origin access, so they have no cookies at all. Instead they call the API with a token the shell hands them, scoped to their application. None of this is exotic. It's the cookie and isolation features every current browser supports, switched on and kept on. ## What about service providers? One kind of organisation doesn't fit neatly: managed service providers. An MSP looks after many organisations with one team, one configuration baseline and one bill, and a separate instance for each organisation it manages doesn't give them that. For them, an instance can be split into **domains**, arranged as a tree: a global root, an optional provider domain, and a domain for each organisation the provider manages. Every user belongs to one domain, and tables that opt in get a domain column, which persistence stamps on every write. The visibility rule is simple to say. You see records in your own domain and the domains below it, plus global records marked as shared. Sibling and ancestor domains are invisible. So the provider sees across every organisation it manages, and no organisation ever sees the others. Configuration follows the same tree. Roles, forms, lists and rules can be defined at a parent domain and inherited, or overridden further down, and the most specific definition wins. An MSP can build an application once and adjust it per organisation, instead of copying it for every one. Domain separation is opt-in per table, and it's off by default. An instance that serves a single organisation keeps everything in the default domain, and the only overhead is one constant column. ## Enforced where it can't be forgotten The domain filter isn't something each screen or API has to remember. It's a predicate that the persistence layer adds to every query through the access module, right next to the role checks. PostgreSQL row-level security on the domain column sits behind it as a backstop, in case a module has a bug. Background work follows the same rule. A queued job carries the domain of the record that triggered it, runs in that domain, and picks up the most specific workflow definition for it. Worker pools can even be assigned to a domain, so one busy organisation can't hold up another's jobs. Across instances you get that for free, of course. ## Domains are weaker than instances, on purpose Domains share a database, so they're logical separation, not physical. An organisation with hard isolation, residency or regulatory needs gets its own instance. Domains are for organisations that are happy to trust the provider's boundary. The price on the platform side is complexity: working out the effective configuration when definitions are inherited and overridden. That's kept out of the hot path by resolving the effective definitions per domain and caching them. ## If you're making the same call Start with isolation from the infrastructure, and add logical separation only where an organisation actually needs it. Going the other way, starting shared and carving out isolation later, means revisiting every query you've ever written.
Peacock: a design system built on web standards
How I put Peacock together: custom elements that work in any framework, framework packages and themes generated from one source, and the rules I wrote down before the components.

import Figure from "../../components/mdx/Figure.astro"; import Callout from "../../components/mdx/Callout.astro"; import PipelineDiagram from "../../components/diagrams/PipelineDiagram.astro"; [Peacock](https://github.com/redvars/peacock) is the design system I created and still maintain. You install it as `@redvars/peacock` and get about 190 custom elements built with Lit, a theme made of design tokens, and generated packages for React, Vue and Angular. The site you're reading runs on it. This is the long version of how it's put together, and why it ended up that way. ## Why I didn't tie it to a framework Design systems tied to one framework tend not to last. A team picks a different framework, or a product migrates, and the components get rebuilt. For a while you maintain two versions that slowly stop matching. There's a second kind of drift, and it happens inside the library. When Peacock reached about 85 components, I audited it and found the same idea spelled many different ways. "Close" alone had eight event names. Each of those is a small thing a developer has to stop and look up. So I had two questions to answer. How can one library serve every framework? And how does it stay predictable once it has well over a hundred components? ## What I wanted from it I held it to four goals: 1. It should work everywhere: plain HTML, any framework, and nothing to install for the simplest case. 2. Each concern gets one source of truth. The component API lives in one manifest, and visual decisions live in one set of tokens. 3. Once you've learned one component, you should be able to guess the next. 4. Accessibility, theming and localisation are there from the start, not bolted on later. ## How it's built ### Components are Lit custom elements Every component is a `LitElement` written in strict TypeScript. Each one lives in its own folder (`src//`) with its styles in SCSS. Shadow DOM keeps those styles to itself, and components talk to the page with ordinary `CustomEvent`s that bubble and cross the shadow boundary. Because they're custom elements, they behave like built-in HTML anywhere HTML works, and a lot of platform behaviour comes along with that. Form fields and toggles are form-associated, so `required` blocks submission, `:invalid` matches, and `checkValidity()`, `reportValidity()` and `setCustomValidity()` work just as they do on an ``. Layout uses logical CSS properties, and the style linter rejects physical `left` and `right` in component styles, so putting `dir="rtl"` on any container mirrors everything inside it. In forced-colors mode, selected and current items switch to system colours. And `data-density` on a container tightens up buttons, fields and table rows. Text gets the same treatment. Every string a component renders has an English default that `setPeacockStrings()` can replace for the whole page, and numbers and dates go through `Intl`, using the nearest `lang` attribute. ### Getting it onto a page The simplest install is two tags: ```html Button ``` `loader.js` defines most components the moment it runs. The heavy ones (editors, charts, calendar views, diagrams) wait until they're needed. A `MutationObserver` watches the document, and the first time one of those tags shows up, the loader imports its module. It also wraps `attachShadow` once, so components rendered inside other shadow roots load the same way. If a page has to stay on its own origin, `loader-full.js` serves icons from the package instead of a CDN. Everyday components arrive with the loader, so they're ready as soon as it runs, and a page only pays for an editor or a chart when it actually shows one. The catch is that nothing is defined until the loader's modules have downloaded. On this site I handle that two ways: `modulepreload` hints fetch the header, icon and button modules alongside the loader, and the hero is plain HTML, so nothing above the fold waits on a component. ### Nobody writes the framework wrappers Custom elements already run inside React, Vue and Angular. What developers in those frameworks miss is the comfortable part: typed props, typed events and two-way binding. Peacock gives them that without anyone writing wrappers by hand. The build analyses the components into `custom-elements.json`, and a generator writes each framework package's bindings from that file. Every prop and event in the bindings is typed. Where a component has `value` or `checked` plus the matching event, they add two-way binding: `onInput` and `onChange` in React, `v-model` in Vue, `ngModel` and `formControl` in Angular. They also register the elements they use, so a framework app never needs `loader.js`. I wrote up the rules this puts on component authors in [Generate, don't hand-write](/blog/generate-dont-handwrite/). ### One theme engine, used twice Visual decisions are design tokens in the [DTCG](https://www.designtokens.org/) format: accent palettes, status colours, spacing, motion, elevation and the type scale. A small theme config picks the parts that vary, like the primary seed colour, the palette variant, the contrast level, the corner shapes and the fonts. The theme engine turns tokens plus config into CSS custom properties. It builds tonal palettes from the seed with Material's colour utilities, then writes the CSS with Terrazzo. It's plain ESM with no `node:*` imports, so the same code runs in Node, where it builds the default `tokens.css`, and in the browser, where it powers the docs theme builder. Whatever the theme builder hands you is exactly what a build would produce for the same config. This site's red theme came out of that same engine. Tokens only help if components actually use them, so two stylelint rules reject raw colours and hard-coded corner radii in component styles. The one exception is a raw colour used as a `var()` fallback. ### The rules are part of the architecture The last layer isn't code at all. Before starting a roadmap that added dozens of components, I wrote Peacock's API conventions down in a decision record. It covers when a mode should become its own component, one event contract for every value control and overlay, one shared vocabulary (`variant`, `intent`, `selected`, `current`, `label`), one size scale, and a deprecation policy. The [case study](/blog/component-api-conventions/) tells the story of that record and what the migration cost. ## The trade-offs | Choice | What it buys | What it costs | | --- | --- | --- | | Custom elements built with Lit | One library for plain HTML and every framework | Components exist only after their script runs, so first paint needs some care | | Framework packages generated from the manifest | One source for the API, so types and bindings can't drift | Component code has to follow the analyzer's rules | | One loader from a CDN, heavy components on demand | One script tag; editors and charts cost nothing until used | Nothing is defined until the loader arrives, so preload what matters | | One theme engine for build and browser | The theme builder and the build always agree | A small engine to maintain | | Written conventions with a deprecation policy | APIs you can guess; reviews check a list, not taste | Renames, and console warnings until people migrate | ## Where it is now Peacock 4.0 brought the whole library in line with those conventions (one event contract, one vocabulary, one size scale, logical placements) and added more than 50 components on top. Later releases have kept to the same rules: 4.3 added the site header and footer you can see on this page, and 4.5 added calendar editing and a calendar timeline. The framework packages still come out of the same build, so nobody hand-writes React, Vue or Angular bindings for a new component. ## If you're starting a design system A few things I'd tell anyone starting one. Write your conventions down early. Around the tenth component, renaming things is cheap. Around the eighty-fifth, it's a migration. Treat the manifest as the contract. If the analyzer can't see something, it isn't public API. Put visual decisions in tokens, and lint for them. A rule nobody checks doesn't stay a rule for long. And bet on the platform. Frameworks come and go much faster than the standards they run on.
Redvars: a modular monolith for a metadata-driven platform
How I'm structuring Redvars: a kernel that owns the only path to the data, modules that extend it, daemons that drive it, and runtimes that decide what each process ships.

import Figure from "../../components/mdx/Figure.astro"; import Callout from "../../components/mdx/Callout.astro"; import RedvarsLayers from "../../components/diagrams/RedvarsLayers.astro"; Redvars is the platform I'm building for enterprise web applications. Teams describe their data, behaviour, access rules and screens as metadata, and the platform turns that into a running, secured application. When metadata isn't enough, they drop down to code without leaving the platform. It's still in development, but its shape is settled, and the shape is the interesting part. This is how it's put together, and why. ## What it has to do The goals are short: 1. Let a team stand up a secure, multi-user business application by configuring, not coding, the common 80%. 2. Give them a way into real code for the other 20%, one that never turns into a rewrite. 3. Enforce security the same way everywhere. No path to data skips authorization. 4. Run locally with one command, and scale out later without re-architecting. There are also things it deliberately doesn't do, at least for now: multi-region active-active deployments, databases other than PostgreSQL, and shared multi-tenant hosting. Every organisation runs its own instance, which I've written about in [One instance per organisation](/blog/one-instance-per-organisation/). ## Interpret metadata, don't generate code The first big decision: table definitions, forms, workflows and roles are stored as data and interpreted at runtime. Redvars doesn't generate source code per application. Interpreting metadata is what lets someone change an app live in the Studio, with no build and deploy cycle, and that's the whole promise of low-code. Generated code hands an app's owners a fork they then have to maintain, and it makes every platform upgrade painful. The cost is an interpretation layer at runtime, which I pay back with caching and compiled query plans. That sounds like the opposite of what I did with [Peacock](/blog/generate-dont-handwrite/), where the framework packages are generated. The difference is who edits the result. Nobody edits Peacock's generated bindings, but a low-code app changes every day. ## A modular monolith Redvars is one codebase, built from separate packages with explicit interfaces. There are four kinds of part. The **kernel** is in every process and can't be replaced. It owns persistence, the security handler, who owns which asset, schema loading, the service registry and the job queue. **Modules** extend the kernel from inside. They add tables, interceptors, data types and services. `identity`, `access`, `apps` and `rules` are all modules, and a module may change what the kernel does. **Daemons** are long-running entry points that drive the kernel: the HTTP gateway, the rules-worker, and later a scheduler. A daemon reaches data only through the kernel's public API, exactly like an outside caller, so it can't get around security. It isn't given a way to. A **runtime** is a named, static list of modules and daemons, built into an image. ### Why not microservices The modules are bound together by transactions. A record write, its permission check and its before-rules have to succeed or fail together. Splitting them over a network early would mean distributed transactions and a lot more to operate, for a platform that has to stay lean. The boundaries are strict all the same. No module reaches into another's internals, and that's exactly what lets the same modules be assembled into differently shaped processes. ### Capabilities, not names The kernel doesn't know any module by name. Modules declare which capabilities they provide, require or can use if present, as typed service tokens such as `AUTHENTICATOR` and `AUTHORIZER`, and the kernel orders them by those. A missing provider or a cycle fails the boot. So a fake, or an LDAP-backed module, can stand in for the real one by providing the same token, and a fake with the right name can't quietly satisfy a requirement it doesn't meet. Two checks hold in every runtime: `AUTHORIZER` has exactly one provider, and `AUTHENTICATOR` has at least one. A process simply can't boot without a security model. ## Two runtimes, one codebase There are two runtimes today. `web` has everything: the gateway, the UI, every module and the rules-worker. It's what you run locally (one `docker compose up` starts it with PostgreSQL and a cache), it's enough for small deployments, and it's the only runtime that serves users. It's also where user writes arrive, so it's where synchronous before-rules run, inside the user's own transaction. `worker` is the headless one. It has the kernel, `identity`, `access`, `scripts` and `rules`, and a rules-worker that runs eight jobs at once instead of one. There's no UI, no gateway and no inbound listener. Its only job is to pull asynchronous work off the queue, so a high volume of workflows can spread across many cheap workers instead of weighing on the nodes people use. | Part | `web` | `worker` | | --- | --- | --- | | Kernel | yes | yes | | `identity`, `access`, `scripts`, `rules` | yes | yes | | `apps` | yes | no | | Gateway and UI | yes | no | | rules-worker | one job at a time | eight at a time | Configuration can switch parts off at boot, but only parts that are in the image. You can't turn a worker into a user-facing node with a setting, because the gateway isn't in it. The attack surface of an image is whatever its composition says. What a process runs is written down in one place and reviewed like any other code. Discovering whatever happens to be installed would make behaviour depend on the environment, and a kernel that names its modules would need a new release every time a module or runtime changed. ## Events as the seam State changes emit internal events: a record about to be inserted, a record updated, a schema changed. Rules and cache invalidation listen to them. Persistence doesn't know rules exist; it just publishes. New listeners, like audit, search indexing or webhooks, can be added without touching the write path. ## Scaling without a rewrite The plan for scaling out is a list of deployment steps, not a list of rewrites: 1. Run several stateless `web` nodes behind a load balancer. 2. Add `worker` pools, and start the `web` nodes with their own rules-worker switched off, so they only queue jobs. 3. Split the worker pools by domain, application or priority, and autoscale on queue depth. 4. Move hot paths, like the workflow executor or bulk data processing, to Rust or Go behind the module interface that already exists. 5. Add read replicas. The query path already tells reads from writes. Each step is either a new composition or an extraction along a boundary the monolith already has. ## The trade-offs | Choice | What it buys | What it costs | | --- | --- | --- | | Interpret metadata | Live changes and painless upgrades | An interpretation layer that has to stay fast | | A modular monolith | Transactions stay local, in one codebase | The module contract becomes an interface that's hard to change, so it's kept small and versioned | | Runtimes as static lists | You can read exactly what a process runs | A new shape of process needs a new runtime file | | PostgreSQL only | Transactional DDL, JSONB, row-level security, one database to run | Lock-in, accepted on purpose | | An instance per organisation | The strongest isolation, and independent upgrades | Tooling to provision, upgrade and monitor a fleet | ## The rule underneath all of it If I had to pick the one decision everything else leans on, it's the one about data: there's exactly one way in, and every caller uses it, whether that's a person in the browser, a rule, a script or the AI assistant. That path, and everything it enforces along the way, gets its own post: [One door to the data](/blog/one-data-path/).
Two rule engines, nine years apart
The small JSON rule engine I wrote in 2017, what it got right and wrong, and how those lessons shaped the rules module in Redvars, the platform I'm building now.

import Figure from "../../components/mdx/Figure.astro"; import Callout from "../../components/mdx/Callout.astro"; import RulesPath from "../../components/diagrams/RulesPath.astro"; In June 2017 I wrote a small [rule engine](https://github.com/shivajivarma/rule-engine) in JavaScript. The idea was simple: describe a business rule as JSON, hand it some facts, and get back true or false. Nine years later I needed a rule engine again, this time for Redvars, the platform I'm building, where rules run around every record write. This post puts the two side by side: what the first one taught me, and how the second one is built. ## The 2017 version A rule was a tree of conditions. The root is `all` or `any`, branches can nest, and each leaf compares a left-hand side with a right-hand side: ```js const rule = new Rule({ conditions: { any: [{ all: [ { lhs: ["student.age"], operator: "lessThan", rhs: 40 }, { lhs: ["student.name"], operator: "equal", rhs: ["user.fullname"] }, ], }], }, }); rule.run({ student, user }); // true or false ``` The one trick I still like is how values were written. A side wrapped in an array is a path into the facts, and anything else is a literal, so `["student.age"]` means "look up student.age" while `40` just means 40. A small `deepFind` walked the dotted path and returned `undefined` if anything along the way was missing. The code handled six operators: `equal` and `notEqual`, with strict equality, plus `lessThan`, `lessThanInclusive`, `greaterThan` and `greaterThanInclusive`, which only compared numbers. In July I converted it to an ES2015 class. ## What it taught me It was a prototype, and looking back, the places where it stopped point straight at the hard parts of the problem. The README sketched where I wanted to take it next: pattern matching, list operators such as `in` and `contains`, and a fluent `.success()` / `.fail()` style for handling the result. The code started with the core comparisons, and `run()` returned a plain boolean. The biggest lesson was about mistakes. An operator the engine didn't recognise, or a typo in a fact path, simply evaluated to false. So a rule with an error in it looked exactly like a rule that didn't match, and nothing told you the difference. Rules over lists, like checking each of a student's subjects, were the other hard part. `forEach` was still a work in progress when I moved on, and it's a good reminder that iterating over collections is where a condition language stops being trivial. A rule engine is a small language. A syntax isn't enough; it also needs something that checks a rule before it runs, so a mistake shows up as an error instead of a rule that quietly never fires. ## What a platform needs from rules Redvars lets teams build business applications from metadata, and rules are how they add behaviour without writing a service. When a P1 network incident comes in, assign it to the network on-call. When a task is created, make its subtasks. Nobody calls these rules from application code. They have to run around every write to a table, whoever makes it, without becoming a way around security. That changes the shape of the problem. A rule now has to say when it runs, not just whether it matches. ## How the Redvars rules module works ### A rule says when, whether and what A rule names a table, the operations it watches (create, update, delete), a phase (before or after the write) and an order. Its condition says whether it applies. Its actions say what happens: set fields, reject the write, run a script, or call a tool that another module provides. ```ts // a rule { name: "P1 to on-call", table: "acme_itsm.incident", operations: ["create"], phase: "before", order: 10, condition: { all: [ { field: "priority", op: "is", value: { const: 1 } }, { field: "category", op: "is", value: { const: "network" } }, ] } } // its action { type: "set", config: { values: { assigned_to: { const: "" } } } } ``` The condition tree will look familiar. It's the 2017 idea, grown up: `all`, `any` and now `not`, with leaves that compare a field to an operand. Operands say exactly where a value comes from: a constant, another field, the field's previous value, the caller's identity, or the current time with an offset. A field path can walk up to three references (`team.manager`), and it reads them as the caller, so a reference you're not allowed to read reads as empty. Rules can also be grouped. A group runs every member whose condition holds, or only the first one, so a member with no condition placed last works as an "otherwise". ### Operators belong to types Which operators a condition can use depends on the column's type. Every type gets `is`, `is_not`, `is_empty`, `is_not_empty`, `changes`, `changes_to` and `changes_from`. Text adds things like `contains` and `starts_with`, numbers add `between` and `at_least`, dates add `within_last` and `within_next`. A secret column offers no operators at all, so no condition can read one. The `changes` family is the one I wish I'd had in 2017. It lets a rule react to a value moving, like a status becoming Closed, rather than to whatever the value happens to be. ### Checked when it's saved, not when it runs This is where that first lesson landed. Every write to the rules tables goes through checks that refuse anything that wouldn't run: a missing table or phase, a condition that reads a column that doesn't exist or uses an operator its type doesn't have, an action of an unknown type, or one that can't run in that phase. The refusal comes back as a validation error, with one message per problem. A broken rule can't be saved, so it can't sit there quietly never firing. ### Where rules run Sync rules run inside the caller's transaction. A before-rule sees what earlier rules set, and a rejection stops the rest and fails the write. Sync after-rules run once the row is written, still in the same transaction, so if one of them fails, the row rolls back too. Async after-rules are for work that shouldn't slow the save down, like creating those subtasks. Each one becomes a job on the kernel's queue, written in the same transaction as the record, so a write that rolls back queues nothing. After commit, the rules-worker daemon claims the job and runs it once, in a transaction of its own. If anything fails, it all rolls back and the run is recorded as failed; it isn't retried. If a worker dies mid-run, the work rolls back with it and the job runs one more time. And a rule whose last ten async runs all failed gets suspended, so a broken rule stops piling up failures. An async rule's writes happen together or not at all, and the job is marked done in that same transaction. A rule author never has to clean up after a half-finished run. ### Guard rails Sync rules sit in the save path, so they get budgets. A script gets 50 ms of CPU, 200 ms of wall time and 20 platform calls, and all the rules of one write share 500 ms. Rules whose writes trigger more rules can nest eight deep, and a rule never runs again on a record it's already running on. Going over a limit fails the write with an error that names the rule, or the chain. ### Seeing what happened Every async run, every failed sync run, and every run of a rule with tracing switched on is written to a `rule_runs` table, on a connection of its own, so a failure that rolls the write back still leaves a record. On a traced request, an administrator can see each rule that ran, how long it took, which actions it took, and its scripts' log lines. ### Everything else is a tool There are only four action types. Anything another module wants to offer a rule, it offers as a tool, which means a rule, a flow, an AI agent and an MCP client all reach that capability the same way. ## Still to come The module isn't finished. Scheduled rules, starting a flow from a rule, rules on other applications' tables, and a visual builder in the system UI are all still on the list. ## What nine years changed Side by side, the condition tree barely changed. Nested `all` and `any` with simple comparisons at the leaves was a good idea in 2017, and it still is. Everything around it changed. The first engine answered one question: does this rule match these facts? A platform's engine also has to answer when it runs, as whom, in which transaction, what happens when it fails, and how anyone finds out. Most of the work in the new module went into those answers.
